U.S. LNG Flows Hit Record High as Global Gas Supply Crisis Deepens

What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,…

U.S. LNG flows jumped to an all-time high this weekend as various projects ramp up production and shipments to markets in Europe and Asia that are reeling from the supply shock in the Middle East.

Pipeline flows to U.S. LNG facilities surged to a record high of 21.8 billion cubic feet on Saturday, up by 12% from this time last year, data from BloombergNEF showed on Monday.

Estimated pipeline gas flows to the Golden Pass project hit a record high this weekend, while pipeline flows to Sabine Pass soared to their highest level since April 2026, per the BloombergNEF data.

Several new U.S. projects have ramped up capacity, and existing liquefaction trains have boosted overseas shipments as Europe and Asia are competing for every spot LNG cargo not needing to transit the Strait of Hormuz.

The war in Iran has significantly reduced Qatar’s LNG exports, which have to move through the chokepoint to reach Europe or Asia.

U.S. LNG exports averaged 17.4 billion cubic feet per day (Bcf/d) in the first six months of the year, a 23% surge compared to the same period in 2025, as export capacity additions from startup production at new terminals and expansions at existing terminals boosted LNG shipments, EIA data showed in September.

Increased U.S. LNG exports could be some relief to the strained European market, which faces the winter without Qatari supply, a ban on Russian LNG imports as of January 1, 2027, and the lowest level of gas in storage sites ahead of winter proper.

Europe remains in a vulnerable gas supply position ahead of winter as LNG flows from the Strait of Hormuz are still way below pre-war levels and QatarEnergy has extended the force majeure on deliveries until the end of December 2026, at the very least.

EU gas storage sites were 70.5% full as of November 14, per data from Gas Infrastructure Europe, well below the five-year average for this time of the year. As temperatures drop and the heating season begins, the storage levels have started to fall as withdrawals have begun in most EU countries.
